corpus.note: Candidates in candidates.json were captured by replaying the production FTS path (searchsql.SQLiteBackend.Query with rank.FetchLimit(10)) against that graph. The capture is frozen: it never re-reads a database, so a metric change is attributable to the ranker alone.

authorship.caveat: The same author wrote the ranker and these judgments, so the set cannot prove the ranking is good. It can prove a later change made it worse. Expectations are never edited to make a run pass; a failing query is either a real defect or a documented disagreement.

Someone asking about discovery wants to learn what package discovery is here: the interface that names the idea, and the file that holds it. The nine language-specific implementations are what that idea expands into, not the answer to the question. An earlier judgment said this query existed to 'test the free-prefix rule', which is a scoring rule and not something a person wants; the list has to answer what the person wanted. Two problems sit behind it. treesitter.PackageDiscovery, the interface, is not in the candidate pool at all, so retrieval loses it before any ranking runs. And the pool holds nine near-identical siblings that fill the top of the result on their own.

A three-letter acronym naming a whole adapter. The package node is the answer; nothing smaller is. An earlier judgment also accepted mcp/deps.go, which cannot be defended: the pool holds about twenty-five files from that same package and deps.go is not distinguished from any of them. Judging one and not its siblings measured nothing. The package node is not in the candidate pool, so this query is now a retrieval finding, not a ranking one: no reordering can answer it while the only correct node never arrives.

Deliberately unsupported, kept red on purpose. No node is named cfg — it only ever appears as a local variable, and locals are not indexed — so the query can only be answered by guessing that cfg means config. Measured over the whole graph, cfg scores config 0.28 against a 0.08 ceiling for unrelated junk: a margin too thin to build a gate on.

Written as one word by the user, stored as three spellings in the graph: ParseCache, parsecache.go, parse_cache.go. Tests that case and separator style do not decide the answer. Filed under subword, not abbreviation: nothing is abbreviated, only respelled, and averaging it with cfg made the abbreviation bucket read 0.500 when the two queries measure different things.

Deliberately unsupported, kept red on purpose. Dropped an 'i', which subsequence matching still sees, so this one is reachable — but only through the qualified name; FTS returns no candidate for it at all. See the bucket note.

Deliberately unsupported, kept red on purpose. Swapped 'ie' for 'ei'. A transposition breaks the ordered subsequence outright, so no amount of ranking can recover it — only edit-distance matching could, and that was removed.

The package name narrows a feature that exists in four packages. An earlier judgment accepted only the contents of crossref.go, which drew the line at a filename the query never mentions: graphgorm.crossRefEdges is in the named package and is about cross-references, so it satisfies both words as well as anything in crossref.go does.
Both words are in the identifier and one is in the path.

Two words describing a shape rather than naming a symbol. Both answers were read in the source, not taken from their summaries: queue.go:206-208 starts `workers` goroutines running q.worker(), and build.go:335-362 spawns workerCount goroutines draining a jobs channel. Neither node carries the words in its name or its path, so today both score zero on name and zero on path and the retrieval order alone decides. The pool holds two candidates and both are relevant, so this query records the shape; it cannot discriminate between rankings.

Describes what the code does. These two are the graph walks that take explicit caps; the other three candidates in the pool report or configure a bounded walk rather than performing one. Both answers spell Bounded in their names, so name evidence already reaches them.

queries.query: how does the graph get built
queries.why: A whole question, the shape a person or an agent types when it does not know the symbol name. Build is the full-build entry point (build.go:155: walks source files, stores parsed graph data, rebuilds search docs). Retrieval returns nothing for it today and the cause is measured, not guessed: SanitizeFTS5 joins its terms with a space (sanitize.go:47), and a space is FTS5's implicit AND, so all six words must appear in one document. Every query of five words or more tested against this graph returned zero candidates. No ranking change can move this query; it goes red until retrieval changes.

queries.query: what happens when a webhook arrives
queries.why: ServeHTTP is the entry point a push event lands on: it validates the event and dispatches repository sync. Zero candidates today for the same reason as the other question queries.

queries.query: where do search results get ranked
queries.why: Rerank is the single ordering entry point; every search path funnels into it. Zero candidates today.

queries.query: how do i follow a call chain
queries.why: Describes call-flow tracing without using the words trace or flow, which is the point: the searcher does not know the name. Zero candidates today.

queries.query: what stops the server accepting new work
queries.why: Shutdown stops accepting new work and waits for workers to finish or time out (queue.go:259-262). Zero candidates today.

A type name typed on its own. The type itself is the obvious answer, and its exported methods are what the type is for: naming a type is how a searcher asks what it can do. Written before measuring, and expected red today: the ranker scores a node's own name and the last segment of its qualified name, both of which are the method name, so the receiver type never enters the score and SyncQueue.Add looks unrelated to the word syncqueue.

The type has exactly two methods and both are the substance of it: ServeHTTP is where a push event lands, verifySignature is the check that runs before anything is trusted. verifySignature is unexported and still relevant — the query names the type, and a reader asking what this handler does needs the check as much as the entry point.

Same shape with a larger method set, so it also measures whether fixing the receiver gap floods the list: this type has nine methods and only these five are its interface. The four unexported ones (rebuildTable, rebuildTableNodes, upgradeLegacyFTSTable, and the rest) are implementation detail of Rebuild and are not counted as answers.
Nothing may be returned. Guards against a scorer that always finds something.
